summary: A revision of RFC 1310 that defines the official procedures for creating and documenting Internet Standards. It is informational. It was replaced by RFC 2026.

eli5.summary: The recipe for how an idea becomes an official Internet rule. This was a revised version, since replaced by a newer one.

questions: what are the standards track maturity levels
subtitle: The IAB and IESG write down how a protocol becomes an Internet Standard, who decides, and how long it takes.

tldr.problem: The Internet community needed one written account of how protocols are standardized, who is responsible, and what the maturity labels mean.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes the organizations involved, three standards-track maturity levels plus off-track labels, the steps of IESG review and publication, and a revised policy on intellectual property rights.
tldr.outcome: It is informational and provisional. It revised RFC 1310 and has since been replaced by RFC 2026.

sections.title: Internet Standards and Who Makes Them
sections.content:
The memo documents the process used by the Internet community to standardize protocols and procedures. It is an activity of the Internet Society (ISOC), managed on behalf of the community by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) and the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG). It is a revision of RFC 1310 and says it is provisional, pending legal review by the ISOC Trustees.

An Internet Standard is described as stable and well-understood, technically competent, with multiple independent and interoperable implementations and substantial operational experience, significant public support, and recognizable usefulness. The stated goals are technical excellence, prior implementation and testing, clear documentation, openness and fairness, and timeliness.
sections.eli5: Before a rule becomes official, many people test it and argue about it in the open, so the final rule is one that really works.

sections.title: The Organizations and Publications
sections.content:
The IETF is a loosely self-organized group of people and the principal body developing new standards; it is organized into Working Groups and Areas. The IESG, made up of the Area Directors and the IETF chair, manages the standards process and gives final approval. The IAB provides architecture oversight and is the body to which IESG decisions can be appealed. The IRTF is not part of the standards process and handles topics too uncertain or advanced for standardization.

Specifications are published as RFCs by the RFC Editor. Standards also receive an STD label while keeping their RFC number. Internet Drafts are working documents with no formal status, are removed after six months if unchanged, and must not be cited as published specifications. The IANA assigns protocol parameters such as port numbers.
sections.eli5: One group writes the ideas, another group checks and approves them, a third watches the big picture, and an editor prints the final book.

sections.title: Maturity Levels
sections.content:
Standards-track specifications move through three levels. Proposed Standard is the entry level: generally stable and reviewed, but implementors should treat it as immature. Draft Standard needs at least two independent, interoperable implementations and sufficient operational experience. Internet Standard needs significant implementation and successful operational experience.

Four off-track labels exist: Prototype (added in this revision), Experimental, Informational and Historic, the last for specifications superseded or obsolete. An Applicability Statement can give a Technical Specification a requirement level: Required, Recommended, Elective, Limited Use or Not Recommended.
sections.eli5: An idea starts as a first try, becomes a well-tested draft, and at last a full standard, like a recipe tested by many kitchens.

sections.title: How a Standard Is Approved
sections.content:
A standards action must be approved by the IESG. A document first stays an Internet Draft for at least two weeks, then goes to the IESG, which may commission independent technical review and issues a last call to the IETF mailing list. The final decision comes no sooner than two weeks after last call, and the RFC Editor then publishes the RFC.

A specification must stay at Proposed Standard for at least six months and at Draft Standard for at least four months or until one IETF meeting has occurred, whichever is later. If a specification remains at one level for twenty-four months, and every twelve months after, the IESG reviews whether to continue. A new version of a Standard goes through the whole process, and the old one usually moves to Historic. Disputes go first to the Working Group chair, then to an IESG member, with appeal to the IAB (section 3.6).
sections.eli5: First everyone gets a few weeks to read it, then a last chance to speak up, and only then does the head group say yes or no.

sections.title: External Standards and Intellectual Property
sections.content:
Section 4 explains how specifications developed by other organizations or vendors can be used in the Internet standards process. Section 5, completely revised and reviewed by legal counsel to the Internet Society, sets the rules on intellectual property rights so that all parties can practice Internet Standards without restriction. It replaces sections 5 and 6 of RFC 1310.

The memo also adds an appeals procedure, an appendix of contact points, and a list of future issues. It states that it specifies no Internet standard of any kind.
sections.eli5: Rules also say that nobody can own an idea in a way that stops others from using the standard.
